name: Media and Behaviour
what: This subtopic examines how print and digital media influence individual and group behaviour through four mechanisms: changes to social connections, social comparison, addictive behaviours, and information access.
why: Media is now inescapable in daily life, meaning its capacity to shape self-perception, social relationships, and access to information affects virtually everyone. Evaluating these influences as both positive and negative is a core critical thinking skill.

items.title: I can distinguish between print and digital media and give examples of each
items.what: Print media refers to information displayed on a physical surface, such as newspapers and magazines. Digital media refers to information projected onto an electronic device, including social media platforms, television, and video games.
items.why: The distinction matters because digital media, particularly the internet and smartphones, has dramatically expanded the speed, reach, and interactivity of information, creating new behavioural influences that print media did not produce.
items.example: A billboard advertisement for a car brand is print media. The same advertisement appearing as a targeted post in a social media feed is digital media, and can be tailored, shared, and commented on in real time.

items.title: I can explain what technological determinism proposes about media and behaviour
items.what: Technological determinism is the theory that technology unavoidably determines cultural and social change, and that the medium itself, rather than any specific piece of content, is what drives changes in behaviour.
items.why: This framework helps explain why the arrival of television, and later smartphones, produced widespread shifts in daily routines and social interaction that no single program or app could account for on its own.
items.example: Families timing dinner around a nightly television program illustrates technological determinism: the behaviour change is caused by television as a medium, not by the specific content of any one show.

items.title: I can evaluate the positive and negative effects of media on social connections at both individual and group levels
items.what: Positive effects include expanded ability to maintain relationships across distances and access online support. Negative effects include social fatigue from pressure to stay constantly connected, the formation of shallow online relationships that produce feelings of isolation, and the risk of false or unsafe online identities.
items.why: Social connections are a fundamental contributor to mental wellbeing, so understanding how media shapes them, for better and worse, is central to analysing media's overall impact on human behaviour.
items.example: On the positive side, around 300,000 Australians joined the 2019 climate strike, a gathering largely organised via social media. On the negative side, large online group chats can pressure individuals to participate in cyberbullying to match the behaviour of others in the group.

items.title: I can define social comparison and explain how media can produce both high and low self-esteem
items.what: Social comparison is the tendency to measure one's own self-worth by comparing oneself to others. Media can trigger upward comparisons to idealised or curated profiles, producing lower self-esteem, or downward comparisons to others with less skill or experience, producing higher self-esteem.
items.why: Because social media platforms encourage users to present idealised versions of themselves, the comparisons they invite are often unrealistic, creating a measurable risk of body-image anxiety and low self-worth, particularly in susceptible groups.
items.example: An experienced hiker who sees beginners starting out on social media may feel confident about their own skill level. However, a person with low body confidence who regularly sees filtered model images in advertisements may experience increased body-image anxiety, as found by Dittmar and Howard in 2004.

items.title: I can define addictive behaviours in the context of media and explain the role of attentional bias
items.what: Addictive behaviours are behaviours associated with dependence on a particular stimulus despite negative consequences. In a media context, an addictive behaviour might involve continuing to play online games during class despite falling behind. Attentional bias occurs when addictive stimuli, or cues associated with them, distract attention away from other tasks.
items.why: While debate remains about whether media such as social media is inherently addictive, the concept of attentional bias helps identify when media use has crossed from habitual engagement into a pattern that impairs functioning.
items.example: A student who is addicted to a mobile game may find their attention pulled toward their phone every time a notification sound plays during class, even when they intend to focus on the lesson. This captures the nature of attentional bias in media addiction.

items.title: I can assess information access as both a positive and negative influence of media on behaviour
items.what: Information access refers to how easily information can be reached by different people. Digital media has made this faster and more widespread than ever before, enabling rapid responses to emergencies and personal research. However, the same infrastructure allows misinformation to spread without restriction.
items.why: The speed of digital information transmission can save lives in medical emergencies but can also cause significant harm when false information, such as unproven health claims during a pandemic, spreads before it can be corrected.
items.example: During the early COVID-19 pandemic, false claims that sipping water every 15 minutes would prevent infection spread widely on social media, giving some people false reassurance and potentially reducing uptake of evidence-based protective measures.
